To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
phorbol myristyl acetate, diocotanoylglycerin, and phosphatidylic acid inhibit the hydrosmotic effect of vasotressin on rabbit collecting tubule.
phorbol esters, dioctanonylglycerol, phosphatidic acids, and 8-p-chlophenylthio-cAMP inhibit the hydroosmosis induced by arginine vasopressin in the cortical collecting duct.
PMA, DiC8, and PA inhibit the increase in hydraulic conductivity induced by AVP in rabbit cortical collecting tube.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of the hydroosmolar effect of vasopresin (AVP) in the rabbit cortical collecting tubules (CCT).
the role of PKC in mediating AVP-induced water transport in rabbit CCT.
the mechanism of action of vasopressine in the cortical collecting tubule, a nephron segment in which vasopressine is known to act as an antidiuretic agent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PKC plays an inhibitory role in the hydroosmolic effect of AVP in CCT.
the PKC system may modulate the hydroosmolic effect of AVP in CCT.
the PKC system is involved in the regulation of the hydroosmoric effect of AVP in CCT, although it is not clear whether the effect is a direct or an indirect one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PKC may be a key regulator of the hydroosmoric response of CCT to AVP.
the hydroosmolar effect of AVP is regulated by PKC and that PKC activation may be an important regulatory mechanism of the AVP-stimulating pathway.
PKC may play a role in the regulation of vasopressinic action in CCT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PKC plays a significant role in modulating the AVP-induced increase in Lp.
the PKC pathway is involved in the AVP-induced increase in hydraulic conductivity.
the PKC system plays an important role in modulating the hydroosmoric effect of AVP in rabbit CCT.
